newsitem.title: FRANCE: Europarliament approves food labelling law.
newsitem.headline: Europarliament approves food labelling law.

text.p: The European Parliament approved legislation on Tuesday to strengthen European Union rules on labelling, advertising and presenting foods.
The legislation, deadlocked for many months by a dispute between the parliament and EU governments, is designed to provide consumers with more information about the products they are eating.
It should also ensure the language used on labels is easier to understand.

Euro-MPs agreed to the final text only after winning an assurance from the European Commission that it would draft separate legislation on labelling alcoholic drinks, which are not covered by the rules.
The text also excludes genetically modified foods, which are covered by separate proposals that have not yet been agreed by the parliament.

The new rules, also agreed in principle by EU governments, will oblige food labels to give more information on the sales name of products, their composition and ingredients, and indicate whether they contain starches likely to contain gluten.
Information about starches is important for people who are allergic to gluten.

Under a compromise text, countries may insist that labels carry "descriptive information" as well as the product's sales name. But they cannot oblige manufacturers to include information about a product's content in the sales name itself.

This follows a ruling by the European Court of Justice in October rejecting a German demand that imports of barnaise sauce not made with butter in the traditional German way be labelled "barnaise sauce made with vegetable oil".

The text exempts manufacturers from indicating the quantity of an ingredient which appears in a product's name when this does not serve to distinguish the foodstuff from a similar product and has no influence on the consumer's choice.
Thus they will not have to detail the amount of malt in their "malt whisky" but will have to say how much salami is in their "salami pizzas".
EU states will have to ban the sale of products which do not conform to the new rules three years after the law comes into force.
But goods labelled before that date can still be sold until the stocks run out.
The legislation now goes to EU ministers for formal adoption.
